summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. summary: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. title: Ladybird's first alpha release

summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. summary: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. summary: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research
